To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the sliding surfaces of Tennessee Sandstone are covered with a glass-indurated gouge, which (2) consists of three types of glass, which (3) form in a temperature-dependent sequence that is accompanied by a progressive change in friction mode, and which (4) is consistent with the idea that the glass forms by melting during frictional sliding.

the sliding surfaces of dry sandstones are indurated by a glass matrix that is produced during frictional sliding and that the nature of the glass matrix is related to the temperature of the experiment, the sliding mode, and the coefficient of sliding-friction.
silica–fusion temperatures occur during frictional sliding on quartzose gouge, and that these temperatures increase as the temperature of the experiment is increased.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of the deformation of sandstones under conditions of high temperature, low confining pressure, and high shear stress.
a particular class of fault gouges, those that are composed of quartz grains that have been fused into a matrix of optically isotropic, silica glass.
the effects of temperature, pressure, and sliding rate on the nature of the sliding surface and the sliding mode in sandstone.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
glass-indurated gouge is a function of temperature and pressure, and that it is accompanied by changes in frictional sliding mode.

the glass-indurated gouge forms by local fusion of quartz grains during sliding, that this fusion is a function of temperature, pressure, and sliding rate, and that the fused gouge is a function of these parameters and of the local stress field.

frictional sliding at low confining pressures is accompanied by the formation of a silica-rich glass, and that this glass has a profound effect on the sliding mode, the friction coefficient, and the nature of the deformation of gouge.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the glass-indurated gouge is a product of local silica fusion and is associated with stick-slip and episodic sliding.
frictional heating is sufficient to produce glass at low temperatures and high confining pressure, and at high temperature and low confining pressure, but not at intermediate conditions.
frictional heating and local silica–fusion are important in the evolution of fault-zone gouges and in the frictional behavior of fault zones.
The main takeaway from our work is that
silica fusion occurs at the sliding surfaces of sandstone during frictional sliding and that the nature of this silica fusion is a strong function of temperature.
the friction coefficient is a function of the temperature at which the sliding occurs.

silica fusion is a likely cause of the increase in the coefficient friction at elevated temperatures and that the nature of the glass-indurated gouge may provide a means of distinguishing between the various sliding modes.
